summary: Redwood ran an Optimize walkthrough focused on session-affinity strategies (per-user sessionization), batching economics, and KV/prefix prefetch tradeoffs. We aligned on initial assumptions for hit rates and latency SLOs; agreed next steps to exchange traffic samples and a cost spreadsheet to model dedicated vs hosted choices.
header: Date: 2026-03-30 15:00 PDT | Duration: 46m | Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Devon Patel (Redwood SE), Oliver Grant (Summit CTO), Priya Nair (ML Eng), Liam Brooks (Infra), Zoe Kim (Product)
transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. we're gonna run through an Optimize-style walkthrough: session affinity, batching econ, and KV/prefix prefetch tradeoffs — should be about 45 minutes. if we need more time we can schedule a follow-up.
[00:07] Oliver (Summit): Great, thanks. we've been trying to get our latency under 250ms p95 while keeping cost reasonable, so curious how session affinity will help.
[00:14] Devon (Redwood SE): cool. quick q — what's your current qps shape? is it many short sessions or long multi-turn sessions?
[00:20] Priya (Summit): Mostly long sessions for chat-support — users ask follow-ups, average session length is about 7 turns, peaks at 120 qps across three regions.
[00:28] Liam (Summit Infra): And infra-wise we have VPC, prefer private connectivity; security's strict — SOC2 in progress and we use customer KMS for secrets.
[00:35] Maya: perfect. so we'll assume session affinity (sticky routing) so KV cache lives with the same model shard, which increases hit rate for the KV cache; Devon will walk through the numbers.
[00:42] Devon: right — first slide, simple model: baseline per-token cost for hosted model is $0.0008/token for the generation model variant A, and about $0.00045/token if you run on quantized dedicated nodes. those are ballpark, obviously we can adjust.
[00:55] Priya: wait sorry, are those numbers per output token only or input+output?
[01:01] Devon: good call — that's total token cost (input+output). in cost sim we split them; typical ratio for you we estimated 1:2 input:output.
[01:09] Maya: for session affinity — the key is KV cache hit rate. if your average session reuses past tokens, prefetching the prefix and storing the key-value cache yields big per-token savings because you avoid recomputing earlier layers.
[01:20] Oliver: how big of a hit-rate do you need for it to be worth the memory overhead?
[01:24] Devon: our sim shows that with a 40-50% KV hit rate, you get roughly 30-35% reduction in GPU token compute cost at ~10 concurrent requests per GPU. at higher concurrency (30-50), batch efficiency also improves so savings compound.
[01:38] Zoe: can you explain the difference between prefix prefetch and sessionization?
[01:41] Devon: sure — prefix prefetch is proactively loading the KV cache for a known context (like a user profile or ongoing chat) before the request arrives; sessionization or session affinity is an operational pattern to route a session to the same backend so that cached KV stays warm between turns. they often go together but are conceptually distinct.
[01:56] Priya: ok, we do a lot of user-specific system prompts, so prefetch seems promising. but we're worried about memory blow-up if we keep many sessions resident.
[02:05] Devon: yeah, that's the tradeoff. you can set an eviction policy — LRU by last turn, or TTLs of e.g., 30 minutes. also partial prefetch (only last N tokens) can reduce memory.
[02:15] Oliver: tell us about tail latency — does sticky routing worsen tails?
[02:18] Devon: it can if the session affinity pins to a busy shard, but Redwood's smart routing can move sessions when overloaded and gracefully fall back to compatible model variants. we also have per-request prioritization to keep p95 within SLO.
[02:32] Maya: let me pull up the cost sheet — Devon, you ran a quick sim with Summit's estimated 120 qps peak, average session length 7 turns, input 80 tokens, output 160?
[02:40] Devon: yes, that's the starting point. the spreadsheet (we'll share link) looked at four configs: hosted baseline (no prefetch), hosted+prefetch, dedicated+no-prefetch, dedicated+prefetch+session-affinity.
[02:52] Maya: headline: dedicated+prefetch tends to be cheaper at sustained load because of lower per-token compute and ability to pack batches, but requires commit and extra infra ops. hosted with prefetch still gives big wins without the enterprise commitment.
[03:06] Priya: numbers? give us one example output — say 120 qps sustained, 7 turns, what's monthly cost delta?
[03:13] Devon: rough example: hosted baseline ~$18k/mo, hosted+prefetch ~$12k/mo, dedicated baseline ~$9.5k/mo (with 3-month commit), dedicated+prefetch ~$6.8k/mo. those are illustrative and sensitive to hit rate and batch size.
[03:27] Oliver: hmm that delta looks attractive for dedicated but we need to factor infra + on-call.
[03:31] Liam: and procurement time, yes. also, what about cold sessions? people drop in and out, lots of ephemeral sessions.
[03:37] Devon: for ephemeral traffic we'd recommend hybrid: route ephemeral to hosted (auto-scaling) and pin long-lived sessions to dedicated pools. Redwood supports routing policies per customer and per-route.
[03:48] Zoe: curious — how do you estimate KV hit rate? we don't have a precise number yet.
[03:51] Devon: we use heuristics: repeated tokens, stable system prompt, and user context length. we also instrument session heatmaps — once you share sample logs we can run a quick estimate. in past customers we saw 30-60% hit rates depending on behavior.
[04:06] Priya: ok we'll share anonymized logs.
[04:09] Maya: security quick note: for private deployments Redwood can use your KMS and HSM, and keep logs in your account; we'll send the SOC2 + architecture brief.
[04:18] Oliver: good. can you walk through the concurrency/batching tradeoff? we worry about latency spikes if you wait to batch.
[04:23] Devon: sure — batching improves utilization but increases wait time. Redwood's continuous batching attempts to pack while respecting per-request latency budgets. example: at concurrency 1-4 you'll see small batches (1-2) and lower throughput; at concurrency 8-16 batch sizes hit 6-12 which reduces per-token compute cost. but if your p95 SLO is tight, you can set max wait = 10ms so we won't hold requests long.
[04:45] Priya: do you do adaptive batching based on prompt size? some of our prompts vary a lot.
[04:48] Devon: yes, kernel selection and dynamic batch shaping account for sequence length. longer sequences reduce effective batch size, we account for that in cost sims.
[04:55] Zoe: what's the memory footprint per session? rough order of magnitude.
[04:58] Devon: depends on model and kv length; for our medium models a full-session KV cache might be 20-60MB; you can reduce to 5-15MB with partial prefetch. these are rough.
[05:09] Liam: so keeping 10k sessions active would be huge. how do you manage that?
[05:13] Devon: that's where eviction policies, TTLs, and tiered caching come in — hot sessions pinned to GPUs, warm sessions stored in a faster RAM cache on edge nodes, cold stored in a compact serialized form that can be rehydrated. there are tradeoffs.
[05:26] Oliver: are there specific knobs in the Console/Optimize UI for these?
[05:29] Maya: yes — in the Console you can configure session TTL, eviction policy, prefetch depth, and routing policy. Optimize will recommend settings based on workload profile and cost targets — Devon will demo the optimizer panel.
[05:40] Devon: showing the optimizer: here's the suggested profile for Summit: prefetch depth = last 128 tokens, session TTL = 20m, eager prefetch for returning users, partial prefetch for new users. the sim says this yields 42% KV hit and 28% cost reduction vs baseline.
[05:56] Priya: hmm 128 tokens might be overkill for some flows — can we tune per-route?
[05:59] Devon: absolutely, per-route overrides are supported. you can set route-level policies for the support bot vs knowledge base lookup.
[06:06] Zoe: one more on routing — session affinity requires sticky IP or cookie? how does Redwood implement it?
[06:10] Devon: Redwood supports multiple affinity keys: client_id cookie, bearer token hash, or session id included in the request. for VPC/private deployments we do connection affinity as well.
[06:18] Oliver: got it. what's the deployment pattern for a pilot? we'd like a low-risk path.
[06:21] Maya: typical pilot: 2-week bench + 4-week pilot with a small dedicated pool (or hosted with prefetch) focused on a single product route. gather metrics (hit-rate, p95, cost), iterate, then expand.
[06:32] Liam: procurement question — if we go dedicated, can we do monthly commit first?
[06:36] Maya: usually there's options: monthly for flex (higher unit cost) or annual for discounts. we'll outline options in the quote.
[06:42] Priya: can you show me the sim input quickly? what are the knobs?
[06:45] Devon: sure — here's what we tweak: qps, concurrency per GPU, seq length distribution, prefetch depth, KV hit rate, TTL, batch wait time, model variant (float32 vs quantized). i can run a sensitivity sim live if you want — maybe run a 2-minute sample with your numbers?
[06:59] Oliver: yes let's do that, we have a sample histogram.
[07:02] Devon: okay share the CSV — i'll run a quick sim and narrate results.
[07:07] [file shared; brief pause]
[07:20] Devon: running... initial output: with your real histogram, predicted peak p95 = 240ms hosted+prefetch, p95 = 190ms dedicated+prefetch; cost reductions similar to earlier numbers. hit rate predicted 38% with full prefix prefetch.
[07:36] Priya: that's promising. what's the margin for error if hit rate drops to 20%?
[07:40] Devon: if hit rate drops to 20% hosted+prefetch savings fall to ~12% vs baseline; dedicated still gives 20-22% savings. so prefetch sensitivity matters.
[07:50] Zoe: any notes on telemetry? we want token-level cost breakdown and traceability.
[07:54] Maya: Console provides token-level breakdown, trace links to traces in your observability stack (OpenTelemetry), and per-route cost heatmaps. we can export CSVs or integrate with your cost dashboard.
[08:05] Liam: SSO and audit logs — we need SAML SSO and per-user audit events.
[08:09] Maya: supported. audit logs can be pushed to your SIEM, SAML/SCIM for user provisioning, and role-based RBAC in the Console. we'll add the security appendix to the email.
[08:19] Oliver: competitors — we've looked at MajorCloudAI and OnPremX. quick impression?
[08:22] Devon: MajorCloudAI is strong on running hosted endpoints but less opinionated about prefetch/session orchestration; OnPremX has good latency but requires more infra ops. Redwood's differentiation is the unified controls and automated recommendations for cost-performance.
[08:36] Priya: any gotchas for model switching/fallbacks? we sometimes need to fallback to a smaller model under load.
[08:41] Devon: we support automatic fallback policies: if your preferred variant is saturated we can route to a compatible quantized variant, preserving semantics with some quality delta. Optimize can simulate downgrade impact on token cost and quality.
[08:54] Zoe: cool. what do you need from us next week to run deeper sims?
[08:57] Maya: anonymized request traces, token distributions, and a list of high-priority routes. also confirmation if you want a small dedicated pool for pilot.
[09:06] Oliver: we'll gather those.
[09:09] Maya: ok quick recap: Redwood to share cost spreadsheet and SOC2/security appendix by 2026-04-02; Devon will run a more detailed sim with Priya's logs and send results by 2026-04-03; Summit to decide pilot pool size by 2026-04-06. any other items?
[09:25] Priya: one ask — can you include a comparison sheet for per-region pricing? multi-region impacts our egress costs.
[09:30] Devon: yes, we'll add regional egress and multi-region replication costs.
[09:34] Oliver: thanks everyone. that's helpful. we'll follow up after internal sync.
[09:38] Maya: thanks — we'll email notes and links.
[09:41] [call ends]
